passages.title: Keeping traditional skills alive
passages.text:
[A] In many countries, traditional crafts such as weaving, pottery and woodcarving are disappearing. The reasons are similar almost everywhere: factory-made goods are cheaper, young people move to cities in search of better-paid work, and the long training needed to master a craft does not fit modern lifestyles. When the last skilled practitioners in a community retire, knowledge that has been passed down for generations can vanish within a few years.

[B] One response has been the creation of apprenticeship schemes in which experienced craftspeople are paid to train young learners. In the fictional region of Calda, a programme launched eight years ago has trained more than one hundred and twenty apprentices in twelve different crafts. Each apprentice works alongside a master for two years and receives a small monthly allowance, which allows them to concentrate on learning rather than taking other jobs.

[C] The programme’s organisers admit that not every apprentice continues in the craft. Around sixty per cent are still working in their chosen craft three years after finishing, a figure the organisers consider encouraging. Those who leave often say that it was difficult to earn enough money from selling their products, particularly in the first years before they had built up regular customers.

[D] To address this, the region has opened a shop and an online store where apprentices and former apprentices can sell their work together. Some have also found new markets by combining traditional techniques with modern designs – for example, using traditional weaving patterns to make laptop cases or phone covers. Purists sometimes criticise such products, arguing that they weaken the tradition. Others reply that crafts have always changed over time, and that a craft which nobody buys cannot survive.

[E] Schools in Calda have also become involved. Since the programme began, local primary schools have invited craftspeople to give regular workshops, so that children can try weaving or carving for themselves. Teachers report that these sessions are among the most popular activities of the year, and a few former pupils have later applied to become apprentices themselves.

coach.message: Bài “Skimming and verifying paraphrases”: Đọc lướt ý chính rồi quay lại bằng chứng thay vì chọn theo một từ trùng. Trước khi thử, hãy nói một việc bạn sẽ kiểm tra ở bài này.

Bạn đang xem “hand down a craft” (verb phrase), nghĩa là “truyền lại nghề thủ công”. Ví dụ: “Grandparents hand down a craft to younger people.”. Hãy tạo một câu mới liên quan đến skimming and verifying paraphrases thay vì chép lại.
Ở ví dụ có hướng dẫn “Why were classes introduced?”, hãy làm bước này trước: Skim for purpose first, then verify the paraphrase phrase by phrase. Chỉ mở mẫu sau khi tự thử.

Lỗi dễ gặp ở bài “Skimming and verifying paraphrases”: Không chọn “to sell more baskets” vì đoạn không nói doanh số. Few apprentices = thiếu người theo học; classes = lớp truyền dạy, nên mục đích là thu hút người mới.

Bạn đã hoàn thành bài “Skimming and verifying paraphrases”. Hãy đánh dấu bằng chứng trong văn bản; lưu cụm “hand down a craft” nếu thực sự muốn dùng lại, rồi sửa một chỗ chưa chắc chắn trước khi làm bài mới.
Bài này mình luyện Skimming và xác minh paraphrase chủ đề nghề thủ công. Hãy đọc đoạn rồi tìm phần nào trả lời đúng câu hỏi; chưa cần đoán ngay.
Bạn đang bị bẫy: People dislike all crafts: không được nêu. Hãy đọc bằng chứng “factory-made products are cheaper and many young workers move to cities” rồi thử lại.
Hãy phân biệt: NOT GIVEN: bài đã có số 96 cụ thể. Bằng chứng cần đối chiếu là “enrolled 96 apprentices”.
Bạn đã tìm đúng cả hai bằng chứng. Hãy vào phần luyện độc lập; Coach sẽ không tự chen vào.
